theme: Asaph was nearly slipping; then he entered the sanctuary
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 73. A believer almost loses his faith because the wicked seem to prosper. You have read this psalm before. Read it now as the prayer of someone in exile, who has lost the temple but finds God’s presence anyway.
settingTheScene: Psalm 73 is the first psalm of Book 3, a psalm of Asaph. It begins with a confession: “But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled.” The psalmist envied the arrogant when he saw their ease. The turning point is when he entered “the sanctuary of God.” For the exiles, the question was sharper: what could it mean to enter the sanctuary when the sanctuary was a ruin? The psalm answers that what matters is the presence of God himself.
observation: “Truly God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart” (v. 1).
“But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled, my steps had nearly slipped” (v. 2).
“For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” (v. 3).
“All in vain have I kept my heart clean and washed my hands in innocence” (v. 13).
“But when I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end” (vv. 16-17).
“I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you” (v. 22).
“Nevertheless, I am continually with you; you hold my right hand” (v. 23).
“Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you” (v. 25).
interpretation:
The psalm is autobiographical. The writer was a believer who nearly gave up. He looked around and saw that the arrogant seemed to have no pain. Their bodies were fat, they were free from burdens, they spoke with malice, and they said, “How can God know?” Meanwhile, he had kept his heart clean, and had been plagued all day long. It seemed that holiness was in vain.

This is the question of the whole book of Jeremiah and Lamentations too. Why do the wicked prosper and the faithful suffer? The psalmist says that he tried to figure it out, but it was too hard for him. “Until I went into the sanctuary of God.” In God’s presence, his view changed. He saw the end of the wicked: slippery ground, sudden ruin. And he saw himself. He realized that his envy had made him “brutish and ignorant.” The sanctuary did not give him a theory. It gave him God.

Then comes the great turn. “Nevertheless, I am continually with you; you hold my right hand.” The psalmist realizes that his security was never that he held God, but that God held him. And he declares: “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you.” God is the one thing that cannot be lost. “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.”

For the exiles, there was no sanctuary in Jerusalem to enter. But there was the sanctuary of God’s presence, which Ezekiel had just seen by the river Chebar. To “enter the sanctuary” is to come into God’s presence and see things from his perspective. The psalm ends with a summary: “For me it is good to be near God.” It is a mark of mature faith. The best thing is not the removal of trouble but nearness to God.
connection: Jesus said, “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32). Hebrews 10:19-22 says we may enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus. Philippians 3:7-8 says that Paul counted everything as loss compared to knowing Christ. John 10:28-29 says no one can snatch us out of the Father’s hand. Matthew 5:8 says the pure in heart will see God. 2 Corinthians 4:17-18 contrasts the momentary affliction with eternal glory.
application:
Think of a time you envied someone. Take that envy into the sanctuary of God’s presence in prayer, and ask what he shows you.

Say verse 25 aloud, and ask whether it is true: “Whom have I in heaven but you?”

Thank God that he holds your right hand when you cannot hold his.
prayerPrompts: Confess your envy and tell God where your feet nearly slipped.
Tell him what you saw when you entered his presence.
Tell him he is the strength of your heart.
